n: At dawn on Sunday, the first day of the week, the women return to the tomb with the spices they prepared, intending to finish anointing His body. Christians would come to worship on this day in honor of the Resurrection.

f.w: the first day of the week
f.g: Sunday — later called the Lord’s Day.

n: They find the large stone that sealed the entrance already rolled away.

f.g: Rolling-stone tombs were sealed with a heavy disc set in a groove.

n: Going inside, they find no body. Luke calls Him “the Lord Jesus” — a title of His risen glory.

f.g: This full title first appears in Luke here, after the Resurrection.

n: As they stand puzzled, two men in dazzling clothing appear beside them. Verse 23 calls them angels; the JST describes them as angels as well.

f.g: Clothing gleaming like lightning — a sign of heavenly beings.
At a loss, confused.

n: Terrified, the women bow to the ground. The angels ask: why are you looking for the living among the dead?

f.w: Why seek ye the living among the dead?

n: He isn’t here — He has risen! Remember what He told you back in Galilee.

f.w: He is not here, but is risen

n: He said the Son of Man must be handed over to sinners, crucified, and rise on the third day. Everything happened just as He foretold.
Then they remember His words. Remembering is often the beginning of understanding.
They leave the tomb and report everything to the eleven apostles and the other disciples. These women are the first witnesses of the Resurrection.

f.g: The Twelve minus Judas.

n: Luke names them: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women. Women who supported Jesus in Galilee now carry the greatest news in history.
The apostles think it’s nonsense and don’t believe them. Even those closest to Jesus struggled to accept the Resurrection at first.

f.g: Nonsense, delirious talk — a word used by physicians for the ravings of the sick.

n: Peter, though, gets up and runs to the tomb. Stooping to look in, he sees only the linen grave cloths lying there and leaves amazed, wondering what has happened.

f.w: the linen clothes laid by themselves
f.g: The burial wrappings left behind — no thief would have unwrapped a body.

n: That same day, two disciples walk to Emmaus, a village about seven miles from Jerusalem.

f.g: Sixty stadia — about seven miles (11 km).
Its exact location is uncertain today.

n: They discuss everything that has happened.

f.g: The trial, crucifixion, and the strange reports of the empty tomb.

n: As they talk and debate, Jesus Himself comes up and walks with them.

f.g: Talked and discussed back and forth.

n: But they are kept from recognizing Him. God allowed them to learn from the scriptures before they saw Him with their eyes.

f.g: Held back, restrained.

n: He asks what they are discussing so intently as they walk along, looking so sad.

f.g: What kind of words.

n: Cleopas replies: are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who hasn’t heard what happened there these past days? The irony is rich — he is speaking to the one person who knows best.

f.g: Possibly the same as Clopas in John 19:25.
A visitor or pilgrim.

n: Jesus asks, “What things?” They tell Him about Jesus of Nazareth, a prophet powerful in action and word before God and all the people.

f.w: a prophet mighty in deed and word

n: They explain how their own leaders handed Him over to be condemned and crucified.

f.g: Handed Him over.

n: “We had hoped He was the one who would redeem Israel.” Their hope is in the past tense. And now it’s the third day since these things happened.

f.g: We had hoped.
Many expected the Messiah to free Israel from Rome.

n: Some women from their group have amazed them — they went to the tomb early this morning...

f.g: Amazed, bewildered.

n: ...and didn’t find His body. They came back saying they had seen angels who said He is alive.
Some went to check and found the tomb exactly as the women said — but they didn’t see Him.

f.g: The empty tomb alone did not yet produce faith.

n: Jesus responds: how foolish and slow you are to believe everything the prophets said!

f.g: Here “thoughtless, without understanding” — a gentle rebuke, not an insult.

n: Wasn’t it necessary for the Messiah to suffer these things and then enter His glory? The cross was not a defeat but the path to glory.

f.w: Ought not Christ to have suffered

n: Starting with Moses and all the prophets, He explains everything the scriptures say about Him. The whole Old Testament testifies of Christ.

f.g: Explained in detail.

n: Approaching their village, Jesus acts as though He will keep going. He waits to be invited.

f.w: he made as though he would have gone further

n: They urge Him strongly to stay with them, since it’s nearly evening. He goes in to stay.

f.g: Urged strongly.
Stay with us.

n: At the table, He takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them — the same actions as at the feeding of the five thousand and the Last Supper.

f.w: took bread, and blessed it, and brake

n: Their eyes are opened and they recognize Him — and then He vanishes from their sight.
They say to each other: weren’t our hearts burning inside us as He talked with us and opened the scriptures? The burning was the witness of the Spirit.

f.w: Did not our heart burn within us

n: At once — despite the hour and the seven-mile walk — they hurry back to Jerusalem and find the Eleven and others gathered.

f.g: Immediately; their joy couldn’t wait until morning.

n: Before they can speak, the group tells them: the Lord has really risen and has appeared to Simon Peter!
The two share their story of the road and how they recognized Him in the breaking of bread.

f.g: A phrase that came to describe the sacrament in the early Church.

n: While they are still talking, Jesus Himself stands among them and says, “Peace be with you.”
They are startled and frightened, thinking they are seeing a ghost.

f.g: A ghost, a disembodied spirit.

n: He asks why they are troubled and why doubts are rising in their hearts.

f.g: Doubts, questioning thoughts.

n: Look at My hands and feet — it’s really Me. Touch Me and see: a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones as I do. This is a central witness of a literal, physical resurrection.

f.w: a spirit hath not flesh and bones

n: He shows them His hands and feet, still bearing the wounds of the nails.
They are so overjoyed and amazed they can hardly believe it. He asks: do you have anything to eat?

f.g: It seemed too good to be true.
Food.

n: They give Him a piece of broiled fish and some honeycomb.

f.g: Grilled fish, a common Galilean food.

n: He eats it in front of them — proof that His resurrected body is real and tangible.
He reminds them of His teaching: everything written about Him in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled. These were the three divisions of the Hebrew scriptures.

f.w: the law of Moses, and in the prophets, and in the psalms
f.g: The three sections of the Jewish scriptures: Law, Prophets, and Writings (headed by Psalms).

n: He opens their minds to understand the scriptures — the same gift He gave on the Emmaus road.
This is what was written: the Messiah had to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day.

f.g: Was necessary for, was fitting for.

f.w: rise from the dead the third day

n: And repentance and forgiveness of sins must be preached in His name to all nations, starting in Jerusalem. This is the mission that Luke’s second book, Acts, describes.

f.g: Forgiveness, release from sins.

f.w: among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem

n: You are witnesses of these things. The apostles are called above all to testify of the risen Christ.
He will send what the Father promised — the Holy Ghost. They must wait in Jerusalem until clothed with power from on high, fulfilled on the day of Pentecost.

f.g: Clothed, endowed.

n: He leads them out to the area of Bethany on the Mount of Olives, raises His hands, and blesses them.

f.w: lifted up his hands, and blessed them

n: While blessing them, He is parted from them and taken up into heaven. His final act on earth recorded by Luke is a blessing.
They worship Him and return to Jerusalem filled with joy — not sorrow. They know He lives and will return.

f.g: They now recognize Him as divine.

n: They are constantly at the temple praising God. Luke’s Gospel begins and ends in the temple, bookending the story of God’s salvation in Christ.
